chunks.content: The rise of patient-specific models for human placental biology The placenta is a crucial organ that connects the mother and fetus, playing a vital role in fetal survival and development [ ]. It mediates nutrient and gas exchange at the maternal-fetal interface, regulates immune responses, and produces hormones for maintaining pregnancy [ ]. The human placenta consists of three types of trophoblast cells. Cytotrophoblasts ( CTs , see Glossary) are the highly proliferative stem cell population that can give rise to further differentiated syncytiotrophoblasts (STs) and extravillous trophoblasts (EVTs) [ ]. Abnormal placental function can lead to significant obstetric complications, including recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL) , preeclampsia (PE) , fetal growth restriction (FGR), and placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) [ ]. Placental research is essential for understanding the pathogenesis and pathophysiology of pregnancy-related complications. Although access to human placental tissue is crucial for studying placental development and function, its acquisition and use have been limited by technical and ethical challenges [ , ]. Given the limited availability of early-stage human placental tissue, various in vitro models have been developed to investigate placental development, function, and the maintenance of pregnancy ( ). By adapting the established derivation and culture protocols by Okae et al. [ ], patient-specific trophoblast stem cells (pTSCs) have been generated from various sources, including human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs), somatic fibroblasts, CTs obtained after completed pregnancies, and more recently, chorionic villus tissue obtained via chorionic villus sampling (CVS) during ongoing pregnancies ( ). pTSCs can retain the genetic and epigenetic abnormalities of individual pregnancies. By capturing inter-individual genetic diversity, research using pTSCs offers powerful tools for understanding placental development and the pathogenesis of pregnancy-related complications. Although pTSCs are emerging as key models for studying placental development and disorders, their derivation methods have not yet been comprehensively reviewed. In this review, we underscore the importance of pTSCs, evaluate their derivation methods, and provide insights into their applications. The need for pTSCs Placental development and the onset of related disorders are often closely associated with genomic alterations, including gene mutations, chromosomal abnormalities, and changes in transcriptomic and epigenomic signatures [ , ]. Many placental disorders exhibit distinct manifestations influenced by genetic background, immune responses, and environmentally driven epigenetic variation [ – ]. An analysis of the transcriptomic landscape in monosomy X placentas highlights the impact of chromosomal abnormalities on early placental development, suggesting that attenuated cytokine-signaling pathways affect immune regulation [ ]. Placentas with large-scale aneuploidies or copy-number variations (CNVs) are more frequently associated with small-for-gestational-age infants compared to karyotypically normal placentas [ ]. Such complexity is challenging to capture or interrogate using the limited number of available bona fide hTSC lines, which do not fully reflect genetic diversity or the broader transcriptomic and epigenomic landscapes ( ). Relying on these restricted models may undermine their physiological and clinical relevance, as well as the fidelity required to elucidate pathogenesis, predict individual risk, and develop personalized therapeutic strategies. In contrast, patient-specific models can be derived through reprogramming or direct induction from an individual’s cells, reflecting the patient’s genetic and epigenetic backgrounds. While disease-specific models are often developed with a focus on a particular condition [ ], patient-specific stem cells can maintain inter-individual variation even among patients with the same disease. They serve as valuable research models for mechanistic dissection, risk stratification, and therapy development by generating personalized placental models [ , ]. These models offer a precise and reproducible system that allows for systematic analysis of disorder-associated alterations in trophoblast proliferation, differentiation, invasiveness, and immune regulation. Even in the presence of the same mutation, inter-individual genetic and epigenetic differences can lead to varying degrees of cellular dysfunction [ , ]. By leveraging pTSCs, inter-individual differences in susceptibility to placental disorders can be evaluated in vitro . Certain pTSC-based approaches also alleviate ethical concerns and enable longitudinal follow-up of clinical outcomes ( ) ( ). This positions pTSCs as key platforms for placental disease research, patient-specific risk assessment, and therapy. pTSC derivation pTSCs can be generated via : (1) trans-differentiation of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) reprogrammed from patient somatic cells; (2) direct reprogramming from fibroblasts by forced expression of transcription factors (TFs); (3) derivation from CTs after the completion of pregnancy; and (4) derivation from chorionic villi collected via CVS during early pregnancy ( ). pTSCs trans-differentiated from iPSCs (iPSC-derived pTSCs) Earlier attempts at pTSC derivation involved reprogramming somatic cells into iPSCs, followed by trans-differentiation into hTSCs. and (4) derivation from chorionic villi collected via CVS during early pregnancy ( ). pTSCs trans-differentiated from iPSCs (iPSC-derived pTSCs) Earlier attempts at pTSC derivation involved reprogramming somatic cells into iPSCs, followed by trans-differentiation into hTSCs. Dong et al. reported that when naïve human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) or renal epithelial cell-derived iPSCs are cultured in hTSC medium (TSCM), a homogeneous cell population closely resembling bona fide hTSCs is produced, exhibiting similar gross morphology, surface markers, and trophoblast-specific gene expression [ ]. However, this model did not fully recapitulate the developmental continuum from pre-implantation to post-implantation stages, as cells representing the initial trophoblast lineage, trophectoderm (TE) , were not detected during the conversion of iPSCs into pTSCs. iPSC-derived pTSCs (iPSC-TSCs) were transcriptionally most similar to the human post-implantation TE lineage at day 12, with low levels of CDX2 [ ], a TF that is markedly downregulated in CTs as the first trimester progresses [ ]. In parallel, Cinkornpumin et al. showed that naïve hPSCs can be converted to hTSCs [ ]. In addition, their findings indicated substantial differences in conversion efficiency, lineage fidelity, and differentiation capacity of the TSCs, depending on the PSC state and cell lines. Shortly after, Io et al. induced pTSCs that more closely resemble pre-implantation-stage TE from naïve hESCs and iPSCs using the ACE culture condition, which contains A83–01, CHIR99021, and epidermal growth factor (EGF) [ ]. This method established an in vitro model that faithfully recapitulates the complete trajectory of trophoblast development from pre- to post-implantation. The derived pTSCs have met established criteria for human first-trimester trophoblasts, including extended self-renewal, bipotency, lack of HLA class I expression, an active miRNA cluster on chromosome 19 (C19MC), demethylation of the ELF5 promoter, and the expression of GATA3, TFAP2C, and KRT7 proteins [ ]. This approach enabled the derivation of pTSCs from dermal fibroblasts, providing a non-invasive and practical method for establishing pTSCs. A recent study examined whether naïve or primed iPSCs are more suitable for producing pTSCs that accurately model placental disorders ( ). Morey et al. demonstrated that both naïve- and primed-derived iPSCs from PE patients efficiently generated pTSCs [ ]. However, EVTs differentiated from primed iPSC-TSCs, but not from naïve iPSC-TSCs, exhibited pathological characteristics of PE, including reduced surface HLA-G expression, impaired invasiveness, and altered EVT-specific gene expression [ ]. These abnormalities correlated with hypermethylation of promoters of genes involved in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), suggesting that aberrant epigenetic regulation may contribute to the pathogenesis of PE. These findings indicate that primed iPSCs may be more appropriate for modeling PE through conversion into pTSCs. However, as shown in some earlier studies [ , ], primed iPSC-TSCs were deficient in C19MC expression, and the analysis was limited to DNA methylation without examining chromatin accessibility or other epigenetic modifications. This indicates that further research is necessary before firm conclusions can be drawn. Notably, in this study, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) from umbilical cords were reprogrammed into iPSCs and subsequently converted into hTSCs. The use of umbilical cords, which retain genetic and epigenetic information from both parents, offers a significant advantage over skin, peripheral blood, or other tissues for modeling placental disorders. Importantly, iPSCs and iPSC-derived pTSCs derived from placental or fetal cells enable isogenic modeling of both placental and embryonic development. Nevertheless, multistep protocols, prolonged conversion durations, and low overall conversion efficiency remain major challenges for the application of iPSC-derived pTSCs. pTSCs directly reprogrammed from fibroblasts via TF induction (fibroblast-derived pTSCs) pTSCs can also be directly reprogrammed from fibroblasts through ectopic expression of TFs. Liu et al. demonstrated that during the reprogramming of human dermal fibroblasts into iPSCs via the introduction of OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC (OSKM), a subset of cells enters a TE-like state. By capturing and culturing this cell population in TSCM, they derived stable induced TSCs (iTSCs) [ ]. iTSCs expressed key markers of human TE and TSCs, including P63, TFAP2C, GATA2, and KRT7, and were capable of differentiating into STs and EVTs. This study was the first to demonstrate that iTSCs can be directly derived from human somatic cells without an intermediate iPSC stage. Subsequently, Castel et al. confirmed that OSKM reprogramming of dermal fibroblasts, including neonatal fibroblasts, can generate iTSCs whose transcriptomes closely resemble those of post-implantation day 8 CTs [ ]. These findings indicate that iTSCs offer a useful platform for studying early post-implantation trophoblast development. While OSKM overexpression in mouse fibroblasts can activate an initial trophoblast-like transcriptional program during iPSC generation, it does not lead to the establishment of stable iTSCs [ , ], suggesting an intriguing species-specific difference. Notably, stable iTSCs can be generated from mouse fibroblasts through the ectopic expression of TFs, such as Gata3, Eomes, Tfap2c, and either Myc or Ets2 (GETM/GETE) [ , ]. While OSKM overexpression in mouse fibroblasts can activate an initial trophoblast-like transcriptional program during iPSC generation, it does not lead to the establishment of stable iTSCs [ , ], suggesting an intriguing species-specific difference. Notably, stable iTSCs can be generated from mouse fibroblasts through the ectopic expression of TFs, such as Gata3, Eomes, Tfap2c, and either Myc or Ets2 (GETM/GETE) [ , ]. Fogarty et al. demonstrated that the pluripotency factor OCT4 plays a role in trophoblast lineage induction, as OCT4-null human embryos exhibited downregulation of extra-embryonic TE genes such as CDX2 [ ]. Comparative parallel multi-omic analyses subsequently revealed that the molecular trajectories leading to pluripotent and trophoblast states during OSKM reprogramming are distinct in mice [ , ], raising the question of whether a pluripotent state is necessary for human iTSC induction. Notably, the generation of stable iTSCs from mouse fibroblasts through the expression of Gata3-containing TF cocktails is achieved independently of pluripotency [ , ]. Naama et al. demonstrated that ectopic expression of GOKM (replacing SOX2 with GATA3 in OSKM) can also reprogram human fibroblasts into functional hTSCs [ ]. GOKM efficiently generated iTSCs from fibroblasts lacking pluripotency genes, suggesting that pluripotency is dispensable for acquiring the hTSC state. Mechanistic and transcriptional analyses revealed that GOKM primarily targets hTSC-specific loci, whereas OSKM induces the iTSC state by acting on loci shared between hESCs and hTSCs. Notably, OSKM-derived iTSCs aberrantly expressed 94 hTSC-specific genes compared to GOKM-derived iTSCs [ ]. Furthermore, OSKM-derived iTSCs lacked gene signatures associated with estrogen response and immune function, critical processes for implantation and early placental development [ – ]. This study underscored the importance of selecting the appropriate TFs for directly inducing pTSCs from fibroblasts while preserving functional competence. Patient-derived iTSCs offer a unique platform for investigating early placental developmental defects and disorders in genetically diverse patient populations. In mouse systems, the direct conversion of fibroblasts into iTSCs has been suggested to be superior to derivation from pluripotent cells, which can lead to unstable colonies and epigenetic abnormalities [ ]. This advantage may stem from the fact that conversion to iTSCs occurs through a single, lineage-directed step rather than a two-step process. However, iTSC induction still involves epigenetic and transcriptional remodeling, which may compromise epigenetic fidelity [ ]. Importantly, pTSCs derived from maternal somatic cell types do not capture biparental genetic contributions, underscoring the need to consider the cell of origin when deriving pTSCs from iPSCs or fibroblasts ( ). pTSCs derived from CTs after pregnancy completion (CT-derived pTSCs) The direct derivation of hTSCs from primary CTs offers significant advantages for preserving the genetic and epigenetic features of a patient’s placenta. Saha et al. reported the establishment of hTSCs from first-trimester CTs obtained from patients with idiopathic RPLs (RPL-TSCs) [ ]. After initial passages on placental mesenchymal stromal feeders, RPL-TSCs could be maintained in feeder-free conditions and retained normal karyotypes. These cells exhibited reduced proliferation, unstable morphology, and inefficient organoid formation, all of which were restored after the rescue of TEAD4 expression [ ]. This study demonstrated that pTSCs can be established from placental tissues of patients with idiopathic RPL and they effectively model molecular abnormalities not observed in bona fide hTSCs. Early placentas in cases of idiopathic RPL still retain TSCM-responsive villous CT populations. However, Okae and others were unable to derive hTSCs or trophoblast organoids from term placentas using the culture conditions applied to first-trimester samples [ , , ], suggesting that establishing hTSCs from term placentas may require alternative approaches. Bai et al. achieved this by forced expression of CDX2, ELF5, ETS2, TFAP2C, and TEAD4 in villous CTs isolated from term placentas at birth and cultured in a modified TSCM [ ]. The derived iTSCs exhibit transcriptional similarity to hTSCs, can self-renew indefinitely, and are bipotent. Wang et al. also derived hTSCs from term placentas under 1% oxygen in TSCM that exhibited key properties of bona fide hTSCs [ ]. More recently, Karakis et al. derived hTSCs from CTs isolated at delivery using TSCM supplemented with the low-dose mitochondrial pyruvate uptake inhibitor UK5099 and lipid-rich albumin (TUA) [ ]. The addition of lipid-rich albumin enabled long-term culture but produced cells lacking differentiation potential. Only with additional UK5099 supplementation did hTSCs exhibit the capacity to differentiate into EVT and ST lineages [ ]. Similarly, Hoshiyama et al. isolated ITGA6 + CTs from the term smooth chorion and established chorion-derived TSCs (Ch-TSCs) using TSCM [ ]. Ch-TSCs were transcriptionally similar to hTSCs from first-trimester placental villi. However, their transcriptomic profiles differed from those of pTSCs derived by Karakis et al. [ , ], and it remains to be determined which of the two pTSCs more faithfully recapitulates

CT-derived pTSCs allow for the utilization of routinely discarded placentas without the need for further invasive procedures. However, in many placental disorders, trophoblast lineage abnormalities arise early but manifest clinically in mid to late gestation [ ]. Thus, genetic and epigenetic alterations in CT-derived pTSCs may reflect secondary consequences of chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and other pathological conditions rather than primary drivers. Moreover, even in uncomplicated pregnancies, genetic variants in the placenta tend to accumulate over time, and clones harboring advantageous mutations may expand rapidly [ , ]. These factors complicate causal inference and limit the use of CT-derived pTSCs for investigating the pathogenesis of placental disorders. While functional and mechanistic findings from CT-derived pTSCs are applicable to subsequent pregnancies, their utility for individual risk stratification, prognostic prediction, and personalized therapeutic approaches may be limited for patients without plans for future pregnancies. pTSCs derived from chorionic villi collected via CVS (CV-derived pTSCs) CVS is a prenatal diagnostic procedure that obtains placental tissue to assess fetal chromosomal abnormalities and genetic disorders, typically performed between 10 and 13 weeks of gestation [ ]. Varberg et al. established chorionic villus-derived hTSCs (CV-TSCs) during ongoing pregnancy by culturing freshly isolated villus tissue in TSCM, followed by prolonged culture in a modified TSCM [ ]. In clinical CVS procedures, the median quantity of chorionic villi generally ranges from 20 to 50 mg [ – ]. A minimum of 5 mg of chorionic villus tissue is required to provide sufficient material for karyotype analysis [ – ]. Consequently, residual tissue not required for diagnostic purposes may be utilized for CV-TSC derivation. Varberg et al. established CV-TSC lines from 5–10 mg of residual chorionic villus tissue and reported an induction efficiency of 42% [ ]. The ability to derive CV-TSCs from early placentas has significant implications for both research and clinical translation. First, CV-TSCs are considered to faithfully reflect the genetic status of early-pregnancy trophoblasts [ ], allowing for an evaluation of whether genetic abnormalities are a causal factor or a secondary consequence in placental disorders. Second, CV-TSCs can be obtained from early pregnancies without termination and can be prospectively linked to longitudinal data on the occurrence of placental disorders, related phenotypic outcomes, and even post-natal fetal development [ ]. Clinical information, such as the timing of onset and severity of subsequent placental disorders, can be collected from ongoing pregnancies after the establishment of pTSCs and integrated with the characteristics of these cells. As the interval from CVS specimen collection to evaluating the differentiation potential of CV-TSC lines is approximately three months [ ], current applications are more realistically suited for disease stratification, mechanistic studies, and potentially retrospective analyses rather than for real-time diagnostic use. As CVS is performed as a diagnostic test when a fetus is considered at high risk for chromosomal abnormalities or genetic disorders [ ], it is associated with fewer ethical concerns [ ]. The amount of chorionic villus tissue collected via CVS represents only about 0.008–0.10% of the average placental weight at the time of the procedure [ , , ]. Furthermore, CVS is conducted under ultrasound guidance, and the risk of procedure-related pregnancy loss is estimated to be around 0.2–0.3% [ , , ]. Compared to amniocentesis , which is generally performed from 15 weeks of gestation, CVS offers an earlier opportunity for prenatal diagnosis [ ]. Importantly, CVS should not be performed for research purpose, and derivation of CV-TSC lines should be restricted to residual tissue obtained from clinically indicated procedures. The partial allocation of clinical specimens for research may reduce the available sample volume for diagnosis, potentially leading to inaccurate or inconclusive clinical results. Therefore, the derivation of pTSCs from CVS specimens requires strict adherence to established protocols and regulatory standards, including institutional review board (IRB) approval, prior informed consent, and careful management of specimen division and traceability. Given the availability of non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), CVS should not be performed without a clear clinical indication [ ]. Given the availability of non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), CVS should not be performed without a clear clinical indication [ ]. Prospective applications of pTSCs To date, hTSCs have primarily been derived from healthy cells and tissues; however, future efforts focused on establishing pTSCs from patient-derived placental tissues will be important. Studies on RPL and PE-derived pTSCs already demonstrated that pTSC-based platforms can deliver meaningful molecular and functional readouts in disorder-relevant settings [ , ]. Saha et al. established pTSCs by isolating CTs from post-miscarriage placental tissues of patients with unexplained RPL, showing that reduced TEAD4 expression is associated with diminished self-renewal. Furthermore, restoring TEAD4 expression rescued this self-renewal defect [ ]. Morey et al. derived naïve and primed iPSCs from postpartum placentas of patients with PE and generated pTSCs through trans-differentiation, which they used to identify epigenetic defects during EVT differentiation [ ]. Collectively, pTSCs are increasingly leveraged to elucidate the molecular underpinnings and pathogenic mechanisms of various placental disorders [ , ]. A practical next step in extending pTSCs for clinical diagnosis and therapeutic applications is to establish a standardized panel of endpoints across various pTSC sources. This panel should include: (1) ST/EVT differentiation efficiency; (2) functional validation through EVT invasion, ST barrier leakage, and hormone secretion assays; and (3) transcriptomic and epigenomic reference mapping. A systematic comparison of pTSC lines may clarify the factors driving clonal variability among hTSCs, which could stem from differences in clinical contexts, tissue origin and quality, derivation and culture methods, or underlying genetic and epigenetic backgrounds. The establishment and preservation of pTSC biobanks will allow for repeated and expanded analyses from the same resource, unlike conventional biobanks that rely on biospecimens available in limited quantities [ ], providing a critical foundation for future research. CV-TSCs, in particular, can be obtained before the onset of placental disorders and are notable for their capacity to collect additional clinical specimens and data prospectively. Placental disorders causing major outcomes can be assessed within months, while long-term follow-up enables multilayered analyses linking postpartum maternal health, neonatal neurodevelopment, and a wide range of other outcomes [ ]. This could evolve into a novel prospective cohort study leveraging pTSCs. The characteristics of pTSCs can be assessed alongside clinical data such as lifestyle information, blood test results, imaging data, placental pathology, and multi-omics profiles, facilitating a mechanistic understanding of gene-regulatory mechanisms. This offers a complementary approach to current precision medicine and lays the groundwork for personalized strategies in diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. Incorporating pTSCs into trophoblast organoids or placenta-on-a-chip platforms will enhance their physiological relevance and accelerate translational research by enabling mechanistic studies of placental disorder pathogenesis, evaluation of drug responses, screening of therapeutic candidates, and development of gene-based interventions. Trophoblast organoids derived from naïve hPSC-derived TSCs have been shown to replicate the dynamics of the X chromosome inactivation in the placenta and also demonstrate selective vulnerability to both SARS-CoV-2 and the Zika virus [ ]. Successful clinical translation of cell and gene therapies will require process designs that prioritize manufacturability and the implementation of Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP)-based quality systems [ ]. Integrating automation, rigorous validation, and regulatory compliance into standard operating procedures will be critical to success. These advances are expected to strengthen translational pipelines, shifting the traditional one-way trajectory from bedside to bench toward a truly bidirectional paradigm. It is important to note that the efficiency and duration of derivation, reproducibility, and the resulting cell states and functional readouts can vary depending on the starting material and derivation protocols. While CV-TSC lines can be established before delivery, the current window for derivation and functional evaluation extends beyond early gestation, a period during which significant placental development occurs. Additional bottlenecks may include inter- and intra-placental heterogeneity, assay and batch effects, as well as genetic and epigenetic drift that can occur during the prolonged culture of pTSCs. Concluding remarks pTSCs are emerging as an innovative platform driving advances in placental biology and reproductive medicine. They can be established through various approaches, including the trans-differentiation of iPSCs, direct reprogramming from fibroblasts, derivation from CTs after pregnancy completion, and from chorionic villi collected via CVS during pregnancy. CV-TSCs hold particular promise, as they can be obtained from early placental tissue without terminating the pregnancy, allowing for longitudinal studies with prospective clinical datasets. Retaining each patient’s unique genetic and epigenetic backgrounds, pTSCs enable investigations into placental disorder pathogenesis, prediction of individual risk, and the development of personalized therapies. When combined with organoid models and placenta-on-a-chip platforms, their physiological relevance is further enhanced, accelerating translational research that bridges basic and clinical studies (see ). Multiple complementary sources of pTSCs provide powerful toolkits for modeling placental development and disorders. Although there have been numerous reports on hTSC derivation from diverse starting materials and distinct media and TF combinations, the field lacks thorough head-to-head benchmarking. Systematic comparisons across protocols, particularly via transcriptional and epigenomic alignment through bona fide placental CTs, along with the standardization of derivation protocols and differentiation state assessment, will be a key priority. Comparative analyses across pTSC models can help disentangle primary pathogenic mechanisms from secondary adaptations, reveal genotype-epigenotype-phenotype relationships, and facilitate mechanistic dissection across distinct developmental windows. Looking ahead, advances in the field will rely on the standardization of derivation protocols, comparative studies across diverse patient populations, systematic genomic, epigenomic, and transcriptomic profiling, and the establishment of pTSC biobanks. Together, these efforts will address current knowledge gaps (see ) and allow pTSCs to evolve from simple experimental models into indispensable resources for precision medicine in reproductive health, expanding our understanding of placental disorders and supporting patient-specific approaches for the diagnosis, prevention, and management of pregnancy complications.
